L50: # Classically psh and pluriharmonic functions on Berkovich spaces Thanks: W. Gubler was supported by the collaborative research center SFB 1085 Higher Invariants - Interactions between Arithmetic Geometry and Global Analysis funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft.
L51: Walter Gubler Address: W. Gubler, Mathematik, Universität Regensburg, 93040 Regensburg, Germany Email address: walter.gubler@mathematik.uni-regensburg.de and Joseph Rabinoff Address: J. Rabinoff, Department of Mathematics, Trinity College of Arts and Sciences, Duke University, Durham, NC 27708, USA Email address: jdr@math.duke.edu
L52: ###### Abstract.
L53: First we extend the theory of subharmonic functions on smooth strictly $k$-analytic curves from Thuillier’s thesis to the case of possibly singular analytic curves over a non-archimedean field $k$. Classically psh functions are then defined as in complex geometry by using pullbacks to analytic curves (and requiring compatibility with base change). We give various properties of classically psh functions including a local and a global maximum principle.
L54: As a consequence, we show that the space of pluriharmonic functions on a quasi-compact Berkovich space is finite dimensional. As a technical tool, we use that a connected Berkovich space is connected by analytic curves.
L55: ###### Key words and phrases:
L56: 
L57: Berkovich spaces, plurisubharmonic and pluriharmonic functions
L58: 
L59: ###### 1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
L60: 
L61: Primary 14G40; Secondary 31C05, 32P05, 32U05
L62: ## 1. Introduction
L63: Plurisubharmonic functions are the complex analytic counterparts of subharmonic functions in real analysis. To recall the definition, we begin with the notion of subharmonicity on the complex line. Let $\Omega\subset{\mathbf{C}}$ be an open set and let $u\colon\Omega\to[-\infty,\infty)$ be an upper semicontinuous function.
L64: Then $u$ is subharmonic if for every closed ball $\overline{B}(a,r)$ with center $a$ and radius $r$ contained in $\Omega$ and every continuous function $h\colon\overline{B}(a,r)\to{\mathbf{R}}$ which is harmonic on the open ball $B(a,r)$ such that $u\leq h$ on the boundary $\partial\overline{B}(a,r)$, we have $u\leq h$ on $\overline{B}(a,r)$. Note that the notion of (sub)harmonicity is insensitive to biholomorphic maps, hence makes sense on any one-dimensional complex manifold.
L65: Now let $X$ be any complex manifold (without boundary, for simplicity) and let $u\colon X\to[-\infty,\infty)$ be an upper semicontinuous function. Then $u$ is plurisubharmonic or psh if, for every holomorphic map $f\colon B(0,1)\to X$ from the open unit ball $B(0,1)\subset{\mathbf{C}}$, the pullback $u\circ f$ is subharmonic on $B(0,1)$. We say that $u$ is pluriharmonic if $u$ and $-u$ are plurisubharmonic.
L66: Plurisubharmonicity was introduced by Lelong [【38†Lel42】] and Oka [【39†Oka42】] independently to study holomorphic convexity. It turned out to be a crucial positivity notion on complex manifolds. Plurisubharmonic functions satisfy the following properties:
L67: 
L68:   1. (1)
L69: 
L70: The space of psh functions forms a convex cone: that is, if $u_{1},u_{2}$ are psh and $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\geq 0$, then $\lambda_{1}u_{1}+\lambda_{2}u_{2}$ is psh.
L71: 
L72:   2. (2)
L73: If $u_{1},u_{2}$ are psh functions then $\max\{u_{1},u_{2}\}$ is psh.
L74: 
L75:   3. (3)
L76: 
L77: If $\{u_{k}\}_{k\geq 1}$ is a decreasing sequence of psh functions, then $u=\lim u_{k}$ is psh.
L78: 
L79:   4. (4)
L80: 
L81: A psh function $u$ satisfies the local maximum principle: if $u$ attains a local maximum at $x_{0}\in X$, then $u$ is constant on the connected component of $x_{0}$ in $X$.
L82: Now we consider the non-Archimedean situation. Let $k$ be a field that is complete with respect to a non-Archimedean absolute value $|\phantom{a}|$. We refer to Section 【14†2】 for the notions used from non-Archimedean geometry. The theory of subharmonic functions on a smooth, strictly analytic $k$-curve $X$ has been completely worked out by Thuillier in his thesis [【40†Thu05】].
L83: Thuillier begins by defining harmonic functions as certain piecewise linear functions satisfying a balancing condition; see [【40†Thu05】, §2.3] or 【41†3.2】. He then defines a subharmonic function to be an upper semicontinuous function $u\colon X\to{\mathbf{R}}\cup\{-\infty\}$ such that, for every strictly affinoid domain $U\subset X$ and every harmonic function $h$ on $U$ such that $u\leq h$ on $\partial U$, we have $u\leq h$ on $U$.
L84: Thuillier shows that subharmonic functions on smooth non-Archimedean curves satisfy the properties one would expect, in analogy to the complex case.
L85: In higher dimensions, it is not completely clear yet what is the best definition for plurisubharmonic functions. There is the global approach by Zhang [【42†Zha95】], who defines a semipositive metric on a line bundle $L$ over a projective $k$-variety $X$ to be the uniform limit of metrics induced by nef models. This approach is used in Arakelov geometry for various arithmetic applications.
L86: For an ample class $\theta$ on $X$, Boucksom and Jonsson [【43†BJ22】] give a far reaching global pluripotential theory on a projective variety over a trivially valued field. Some parts work for any non-Archimedean field, at least in residue characteristic zero. These psh functions might be singular, and the definition uses decreasing limits of semipositive model functions as in Zhang’s approach.
L87: Chambert–Loir and Ducros [【44†CD25】] have posted a second version of their work in which they give a new definition of psh functions which is functorial and is based on a transfinite regularization process.
L88: In all of the above approaches, a maximum principle for plurisubharmonic functions is missing. In this paper, we propose another class of psh functions called classically plurisubharmonic functions in close analogy to the complex case. The definition is local, the functions are upper semicontinuous, and we will show that properties (【45†1】)–(【46†4】) are satisfied.
L89: It will be clear that classically psh functions form a maximal class of reasonable plurisubharmonic functions that is compatible with Thuillier’s definition for curves. In particular, the psh functions from the above are classically psh (see 【8†1.2】 below).
L90: To get regularization by smooth psh functions in the sense of Chambert-Loir and Ducros or to define a Monge–Ampère measure for psh functions, additional hypotheses as in [【44†CD25】] might be needed, but that is not the subject of this paper.
L91: ### 1.1. Subharmonic functions on arbitrary $k$-analytic curves
L92: In Section 【30†3】, we define subharmonic functions on any $k$-analytic curve $X$ to be the elements of the following subsheaf of the sheaf of upper semicontinuous functions on $X$ with range $[-\infty,\infty)$. It is the smallest subsheaf that is functorial with respect to pullback, stable under base change, and agrees with Thuillier’s subharmonic functions on smooth $k$-analytic curves.
L93: We will show in Proposition 【30†3】 that subharmonic functions satisfy the properties (【45†1】)–(【47†3】) as in the complex case, and the local maximum principle on the interior $\operatorname{Int}(X)=X\setminus\partial X$.
L94: ### 1.2. Plurisubharmonic functions on $k$-analytic spaces
L95: 
L96: We define classically plurisubharmonic functions on $k$-analytic spaces as the elements of the smallest subsheaf of the sheaf of upper semicontinuous functions with range $[-\infty,\infty)$ that is functorial with respect to pullback, stable under base change, and agrees with the above defined sheaf of subharmonic functions on $k$-analytic curves. In Section 【31†4】, we will show that classically psh functions satisfy properties (【45†1】)–(【47†3】).
L97: We use the terminology classically psh to distinguish from the psh functions introduced by Chambert-Loir and Ducros in [【44†CD25】]. Note that psh functions are classically psh. Indeed, psh functions are upper semi-continuous and the definition is functorial, so we are reduced to the case of a smooth analytic curve $C$. We have to see that a psh function is subharmonic. By base change, we may assume that $k$ is algebraically closed and non-trivially valued, see Proposition 【30†3】(【48†7】).
L98: Since subharmonic functions are stable under decreasing limits, and the psh functions are defined by a transfinite regularization process from smooth psh functions, it is enough to show that a smooth psh function on $C$ is subharmonic. This follows from a result of Wanner [【49†Wan19】, Theorem 4.7].
L99: ### 1.3. Plurisubharmonic ${\mathbf{R}}$-PL functions
L100: For an ${\mathbf{R}}$-piecewise linear function $h\colon X\to{\mathbf{R}}$ on a good strictly $k$-analytic space over a non-trivially valued field $k$, we have studied the notion of semipositivity in the paper [【50†GR25】]. This notion is a local analytic version of the global semipositive metrics introduced by Zhang [【42†Zha95】] which are induced by nef models. We show in Theorem 【31†4】 that an ${\mathbf{R}}$-PL function $h$ is semipositive if and only if $h$ is classically psh.
L101: ### 1.4. Connectivity by curves
L102: In Theorem 【32†5】, we show that two points $x,y$ of a connected $k$-analytic space $X$ can be connected by analytic curves (assumed to be compact and defined over a non-Archimedean field extension of $k$). If $\partial X=\emptyset$, then we even show that $x,y$ can be connected by overconvergent curves, which means roughly speaking that we can connect them with the interiors of compact curves. We refer to Section 【32†5】 for the precise definitions.
L103: The proof of Theorem 【32†5】 is inspired by Berkovich’s proof [【51†Ber90】, §3.2] showing that a connected $k$-analytic space is pathwise connected. However, we have to choose different paths, as the ones in ibid are not analytic curves. This result is related to [【52†dJ95】, Proposition 6.1.1] and [【53†Ber07】, Theorem 4.1.1] (see the discussion after the statement of Theorem 【32†5】 for more details).
L104: ###### Theorem \the\thmnumbering (Local Maximum Principle).
L105: 
L106: Let $X$ be a $k$-analytic space, and let $u$ be a classically psh function on $X$. If $u$ has a local maximum on $x\in\operatorname{Int}(X)$, then $u$ is locally constant at $x$.
L107: 
L108: This will be shown in Theorem 【33†6】. For the proof, one may assume that $\partial X=\emptyset$; then we reduce the claim to the local maximum principle for $k$-analytic curves using connectivity by overconvergent curves.
L109: ### 1.5. Global maximum principle for affinoids
L110: 
L111: Berkovich has shown [【51†Ber90】, Proposition 2.4.4] that a $k$-affinoid space $X={\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}})$ has a Shilov boundary, i.e. there is a smallest subset $\Gamma$ of $X$ such that
L112: 
L113:  | $$\max_{x\in\Gamma}|f(x)|=\max_{x\in X}|f(x)|$$  |
L114: for all $f\in{\mathscr{A}}$. The Shilov boundary is finite and can be described rather explicitly. Ducros has shown that the relative boundary $\partial X$ is parametrized by analytic spaces defined over non-Archimedean extension fields. An inductive procedure leads us to a stratification of $\partial X$; we will show in Lemma 【33†6】 that the minimal strata precisely make up the Shilov boundary of $X$.
L115: Using this fact, we deduce rather easily the following global maximum principle from the local maximum principle (Theorem 【33†6】).
L116: ###### Theorem \the\thmnumbering.
L117: 
L118: A classically psh function on a $k$-affinoid space $X$ attains its maximum on the Shilov boundary of $X$.
L119: 
L120: As an application, we will show in Theorem 【33†6】 that a pointwise limit u of a net of classically psh functions is classically psh if $u$ is upper semicontinuous.
L121: ### 1.6. Pluriharmonic functions
L122: As in the complex case, a function $u\colon X\to{\mathbf{R}}$ on the $k$-analytic space $X$ is called pluriharmonic if $u$ and $-u$ are plurisubharmonic. We study pluriharmonic functions in Section 【34†7】.
L123: We will deduce from the above properties of psh functions that pluriharmonic functions form a sheaf of ${\mathbf{R}}$-vector spaces, they are closed under local uniform limits (even pointwise limits if the limit is a continuous real function), they are stable under base extension and functorial with respect to pullbacks, and they satisfy the local maximum principle. As a consequence of the global maximum principle for $k$-affinoids, we will the following finiteness result in Theorem 【34†7】.
L124: ###### Theorem \the\thmnumbering.
L125: 
L126: The set of pluriharmonic functions on a quasicompact $k$-analytic space is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
L127: 
L128: At the end of Section 【34†7】, we will see that under certain regularity assumptions on the $k$-analytic space $X$, pluriharmonic functions are ${\mathbf{R}}$-piecewise linear. We do not know if this is true without the regularity assumptions.
L129: ### 1.7. Acknowledgments
L130: 
L131: We thank Michael Termkin for hinting us to the crucial reference for Lemma 【25†2.11】. We also thank Vladimir Berkovich, Mattias Jonsson, and Alex Youcis for comments on an earlier draft of the paper. We are very grateful to a referee of [【50†GR25】] for hinting us to Theorem 【33†6】.
L132: ## 2. Preliminaries
L133: 
L134: In this preliminary section, we gather the foundations used in this paper. While 【15†2.1】–【23†2.9】 and the notion of the relative boundary in 【25†2.11】 are crucial for the whole paper, the other subsections can be read later when we refer to them.
L135: ### 2.1. General notation and conventions
L136: 
L137: In this paper, $k$ will always denote a non-Archimedean field, that is, a field $k$ equipped with a non-Archimedean complete absolute value $|\phantom{a}|\colon k\to{\mathbf{R}}$, which may be trivial.
L138: The set of natural numbers ${\mathbf{N}}$ includes $0$. We allow equality in a set-theoretic inclusion $S\subset T$. For an abelian group $P$, let $P_{\Lambda}\coloneqq P\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\Lambda$. For a ring $A$, let $A^{\times}$ be the group of invertible elements.
L139: 
L140: A topological space is called compact if it is quasi-compact and Hausdorff.
L141: ### 2.2. Ground field and extensions
L142: The valuation ring of $k$ is denoted $k^{\circ}\coloneqq\{\alpha\in k\mid|\alpha|\leq 1\}$, its unique maximal ideal is $k^{\circ\circ}\coloneqq\{\alpha\in k\mid|\alpha|<1\}$, and its residue field is $\widetilde{k}\coloneqq k^{\circ}/k^{\circ\circ}$. An analytic extension field is a non-Archimedean field $k^{\prime}$ endowed with an isometric embedding $k\hookrightarrow k^{\prime}$.
L143: For analytic field extensions $k^{\prime}$ and $k^{\prime\prime}$ of $k$, there is a joint analytic field extension $F$ of $k^{\prime}$ and of $k^{\prime\prime}$: see 【22†2.8】.
L144: ### 2.3. Affinoid algebras
L145: 
L146: Consider the polynomial ring $k[T_{1},\dots,T_{n}]$ over $k$. For a collection of weights $r_{1},\ldots,r_{n}\in{\mathbf{R}}_{>0}$, the weighted Gauss norm on $k[T_{1},\ldots,T_{n}]$ is given on $f=\sum_{\lambda\in{\mathbf{N}}^{n}}a_{\lambda}T^{\lambda}$ by
L147: 
L148:  | $$\|f\|_{r}=\max_{\lambda\in{\mathbf{N}}^{n}}|a_{\lambda}|r_{1}^{\lambda_{1}}\cdots r_{n}^{\lambda_{n}}.$$  |
L149: We denote by $k\langle r_{1}^{-1}T_{1},\dots,r_{n}^{-1}T_{n}\rangle$ the completion of $k[T_{1},\dots,T_{n}]$ with respect to the weighted Gauss norm.
L150: A $k$-affinoid algebra is a Banach algebra ${\mathscr{A}}$ over $k$ isomorphic as a $k$-algebra to $k\langle r_{1}^{-1}T_{1},\dots,r_{n}^{-1}T_{n}\rangle/I$ for some $n\in{\mathbf{N}}$ and for some (closed) ideal $I$ of $k\langle r_{1}^{-1}T_{1},\dots,r_{n}^{-1}T_{n}\rangle$, such that the norm of ${\mathscr{A}}$ is equivalent to the residue norm on $k\langle r_{1}^{-1}T_{1},\dots,r_{n}^{-1}T_{n}\rangle/I$. If we can choose all $r_{i}=1$, then ${\mathscr{A}}$ is called a strictly $k$-affinoid algebra.
L151: ### 2.4. Affinoid spaces
L152: We denote by ${\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}})$ the Berkovich spectrum of a $k$-affinoid algebra ${\mathscr{A}}$. It is the set of bounded multiplicative seminorms $p$ on ${\mathscr{A}}$ with $p(1)=1$. We usually denote the points of $X={\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}})$ by $x$ instead of $p$, and we write $|f(x)|$ instead of $p(f)$ for $f\in{\mathscr{A}}$. We endow $X$ with the topology generated by the functions $(|f(\cdot)|)_{f\in{\mathscr{A}}}$.
L153: Then $X$ is a compact space endowed with a canonical sheaf of rings ${\mathscr{O}}_{X}$, which we call a $k$-affinoid space. If ${\mathscr{A}}$ is strictly $k$-affinoid, then ${\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}})$ is called a strictly $k$-affinoid space. See [【51†Ber90】] for details.
L154: The Shilov boundary of a $k$-affinoid space $X={\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}})$ is the unique minimal subset $\Gamma$ of $X$ such that
L155: 
L156:  | $$\max_{x\in X}|f(x)|=\max_{x\in\Gamma}|f(x)|$$  |
L157: 
L158: for all $f\in{\mathscr{A}}$. A $k$-affinoid space has a finite Shilov boundary by [【51†Ber90】, Corollary 2.4.5].
L159: The supremum seminorm $|\phantom{a}|_{\sup}$ on $X={\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}})$ is used to define the $k^{\circ}$-algebra ${\mathscr{A}}^{\circ}\coloneqq\{f\in{\mathscr{A}}\mid|f|_{\sup}\leq 1\}$, its ideal of topologically nilpotent elements ${\mathscr{A}}^{\circ\circ}\coloneqq\{f\in{\mathscr{A}}\mid|f|_{\sup}<1\}$, and the canonical reduction $\widetilde{{\mathscr{A}}}\coloneqq{\mathscr{A}}^{\circ}/{\mathscr{A}}^{\circ\circ}$.
L160: ### 2.5. Non-archimedean analytic spaces
L161: The $k$-affinoid spaces form the building blocks for $k$-analytic spaces. Roughly speaking, a $k$-analytic space $X$ is given by an atlas of compact charts formed by $k$-affinoid spaces. We refer to [【54†Ber93】, §1.2] for the precise definition of the category of $k$-analytic spaces and properties. If we can use strictly $k$-affinoid spaces for the charts of $X$, then we call $X$ a strictly $k$-analytic space. A $k$-analytic space $X$ is called good if every $x\in X$ has a $k$-affinoid neighborhood.
L162: These were the spaces considered in [【51†Ber90】].
L163: ### 2.6. Balls and discs
L164: 
L165: We call ${\mathbf{B}}^{n}\coloneqq{\mathscr{M}}(k\langle T_{1},\dots,T_{n}\rangle)$ the closed unit ball of dimension $n$. The open unit ball is the open subset ${\mathbf{B}}_{+}^{n}$ of ${\mathbf{B}}^{n}$ given by
L166: 
L167:  | $${\mathbf{B}}_{+}^{n}\coloneqq\{x\in X\mid|T_{1}(x)|<1,\dots,|T_{n}(x)|<1\}.$$  |
L168: If $n=1$, then we get the closed unit disc ${\mathbf{B}}^{1}$ and the open unit disc ${\mathbf{B}}_{+}^{1}$. The topology of ${\mathbf{B}}^{1}$ can be described explicitly in terms of closed discs ${\mathbf{B}}^{1}(x,\rho)$ and open discs ${\mathbf{B}}_{+}^{1}(x,\rho)$ with center $x$ and radius $\rho$, as explained in Appendix 【55†A.2】.
L169: ### 2.7. Grothendieck topology and fibers
L170: For a $k$-analytic space $X$, we will also consider the ${\mathbf{G}}$-topology generated by the analytic domains of $X$, as described in [【54†Ber93】, §1.3]. We denote this space by $X_{\mathbf{G}}$ to emphasize the use of this Grothendieck topology. For strictly $k$-analytic spaces, we often use the ${\mathbf{G}}$-topology generated by the strictly analytic domains instead: see [【54†Ber93】, §1.6].
L171: In either case, the space $X_{\mathbf{G}}$ has a well-behaved sheaf of rings ${\mathscr{O}}_{X_{\mathbf{G}}}$. If $V={\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}})$ is an affinoid domain of $X$, then we have ${\mathscr{O}}_{X_{\mathbf{G}}}(V)={\mathscr{A}}$. For $x\in X$, we denote by ${\mathscr{H}}(x)$ the completed residue field of the local ring ${\mathscr{O}}_{X_{\mathbf{G}},x}$ with respect to the valuation on ${\mathscr{O}}_{X_{\mathbf{G}},x}/{\mathfrak{m}}_{x}$ induced by the norm corresponding to $x$.
L172: If $V$ is any analytic domain in $X$ and if $x\in V$, then ${\mathscr{H}}(x)$ is the same whether we consider $x$ as belonging to $V$ (which is itself a $k$-analytic space), or to $X$. We call $x\in X$ a rig-point if ${\mathscr{H}}(x)$ is a finite extension of $k$.
L173: If $\varphi\colon Y\to X$ is a morphism, then the fiber $\varphi^{-1}(x)$ over $x\in X$ is an ${\mathscr{H}}(x)$-analytic space, and the underlying topological space has the induced topology [【54†Ber93】, §1.4].
L174: ### 2.8. Fiber products
L175: The category of $k$-analytic spaces admits fiber products by [【54†Ber93】, §1.4]. For analytic spaces $X,Y$ over a $k$-analytic space $S$, we denote the fiber product by $X\times_{S}Y$. Given $x\in X$ and $y\in Y$ over the same point $s\in S$, there always exists $z\in X\times_{S}Y$ mapping to $x$ and to $y$ with respect to the canonical projections [【56†Duc18】, 1.2.13]. For convenience, we repeat the argument.
L176: The completed tensor product ${\mathscr{H}}(x)\widehat{\otimes}_{{\mathscr{H}}(s)}{\mathscr{H}}(y)$ contains ${\mathscr{H}}(x)\otimes_{{\mathscr{H}}(s)}{\mathscr{H}}(y)$ by a result of Gruson [【57†Gru66】, §3.2 Théorème 1(4)], so ${\mathscr{H}}(x)\widehat{\otimes}_{{\mathscr{H}}(s)}{\mathscr{H}}(y)\neq 0$.
L177: The Berkovich spectrum of any nonzero Banach ring is nonempty [【51†Ber90】, Theorem 1.2.1], and any $z^{\prime}\in{\mathscr{M}}\bigl({\mathscr{H}}(x)\widehat{\otimes}_{{\mathscr{H}}(s)}{\mathscr{H}}(y)\bigr)$ induces a point $z\in X\times_{S}Y$ mapping to $x$ and $y$. Note that ${\mathscr{H}}(z)$ is a simultaneous analytic extension field of ${\mathscr{H}}(x)$ and of ${\mathscr{H}}(y)$.
L178: Since Gruson’s result holds for Banach algebras over a non-Archimedean field, the same argument shows that for two analytic field extensions of $k$, there is a joint analytic extension of both.
L179: ### 2.9. Extension of scalars
L180: Let $k^{\prime}/k$ be an an analytic extension field. Then there is a base extension functor $(\cdot)_{k^{\prime}}$ which associates to a $k$-analytic space $X$ a $k^{\prime}$-analytic space $X_{k^{\prime}}$, given on a $k$-affinoid space $X={\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}})$ by the $k^{\prime}$-affinoid space $X_{k^{\prime}}={\mathscr{M}}({\mathscr{A}}\widehat{\otimes}_{k}k^{\prime})$ [【51†Ber90】, §1.4].
L181: We denote by $\pi_{k^{\prime}/k}\colon X_{k^{\prime}}\to X$ the structure map, which is closed and surjective by [【58†GRW17】, Lemma 2.19], [【59†Duc24】, (3.1.1.2)].
